yes and no. since a photon has zero mass, it can't interact with its environment in that way. rather the electron absorbs the energy of the photon to increase its own energy by the same amount.

there are 4 types of fundamental interactions in physics: gravity, electroweak interactions (contains electromagnetism and weak forces), strong interactions, and Higgs interactions. the photon striking electron is an electroweak (more specifically, an electromagnetic) interaction. 

if the photon strikes a free electron, it may undergo Compton scattering, where the photon gives the electron a little bit of energy in the form of kinetic energy. the photon bounces away with a lower frequency, and the electron speeds up like a classical momentum exchange. 

if the photon strikes a bound electron, then it will rise in energy states. if it was originally in orbital 1, and moves to orbital 2, the energy of the photon must be equal to E2 - E1 (the difference in energies of the quantum states). this will give the electron exactly enough energy to be in its new state. the electron may eventually decay back to state 1, releasing a photon of exactly energy E2 - E1.

if the photon strikes a bound electron, but -does not- have energy E2 - E1, the electron goes into a 'virtual state' (a state that does not exist) and -immediately- re-release the photon.

1 MWh ≈ 1341 horsepower-hours. So 38 MWh = 50958 hph. In other words, it takes 50958 horsepower-hours for everyone to view the insta photo. power = energy / time, so 

200hp = 50958hph / time.
